lead: Both readings ask about the inner state of the heart and the eye. Hebrews warns against a heart that hardens slowly, and takes Israel in the desert as its example. Jesus says that the eye is the lamp of the body, and asks whether the light in us is really light. Nearing Christmas, the Church asks us not only whether we are busy for God, but what we are looking at, and whether we can still hear his voice today.

r.h: Today, if you hear his voice
set: The author has just quoted Psalm 95 (Hebrews 3:7–11), with its memory of Israel's testing of God in the desert (Exodus 17:1–7; Numbers 14). The whole generation that left Egypt, except Joshua and Caleb, failed to enter the land. The readers of Hebrews are believers growing tired under pressure, and they face the same danger. This passage is a preacher's commentary on the psalm.
str: vv. 12–14: the warning: encourage one another today; hold firm to the end.
vv. 16–19: three questions and the answer: unbelief kept them out.
kw: The psalm's key word. For the preacher it has not expired: it remains God's “today” as long as this age lasts (v. 13).
The root of our word “apostasy”. It is not a sudden act here, but the end of a slow hardening.
In the psalm, the promised land. Hebrews 4 will widen it to mean God's own rest, which believers are invited to enter.
vv: Take care, brothers and sisters, that none of you may have an evil, unbelieving heart that turns away from the living God.
The danger is described as a condition of the heart, not of the intellect. Note “none of you”: the author is concerned for each one.
But exhort one another every day, as long as it is called “today,” so that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin.
The remedy is shared. Christians are responsible for each other's faith. Sin “deceives”: it hardens without our noticing.
So we see that they were unable to enter because of unbelief.
They had seen the wonders of the Exodus. Having seen wonders is not the same as trusting God now.
ch: The Catechism writes that when the Church celebrates the mystery of Christ, one word marks her prayer: “Today!” (CCC 1165). It also teaches, quoting this same psalm, that it is in the present that we meet God, not yesterday or tomorrow but today (CCC 2659). So every Holy Qurbana is an answer to the psalm: God speaks now, and the hearer responds now.

r.h: Your eye is the lamp of your body
set: Jesus has been speaking to crowds who ask for a sign (11:16, 29). He has said that the only sign is Jonah, and that the queen of the South and the people of Nineveh will judge this generation. The light is already among them; the trouble is in the eyes that look at it. Immediately afterward he eats at a Pharisee's house (11:37). Matthew has similar sayings in the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5:15; 6:22–23).
str: v. 33: a lamp is put where it can be seen.
v. 34: the eye as the lamp of the body: healthy or not.
v. 35: the warning: check your light.
v. 36: the promise: a body full of light.
kw: Literally “single” or “simple”, without folds. It can also mean generous. The undivided eye sees clearly.
An “evil eye” in biblical language often means a stingy, envious way of looking at others (Deuteronomy 15:9; Sirach 14:8–10). So the saying touches both sight and generosity.
A small clay oil lamp, the ordinary light of a house. In the image, the eye does for the body what the lamp does for the house.
vv: No one after lighting a lamp puts it in a cellar, but on the lampstand so that those who enter may see the light.

A note on the text. The POC has “or under a measure” (പറയുടെ കീഴിലോ). Some ancient manuscripts have those words, as in Matthew 5:15, and others, followed by the NRSV, omit them. The sense does not change. Christ is not a hidden light.
Your eye is the lamp of your body. If your eye is healthy, your whole body is full of light;
The problem is not lack of light but how we look at it. The same Jesus was seen by some as God's envoy and by others as a threat.
Therefore consider whether the light in you is not darkness.
One of the most searching sentences in the Gospels: what I take as my light may itself be darkness. It calls for honest self-examination.
ch: St Augustine, commenting on Matthew's form of this saying, takes the eye to be the intention with which we act: if the intention is pure, the whole work is full of light (in substance). The Catechism says that intention lies at the voluntary source of our actions, though a good intention does not by itself make a wrong act right (CCC 1752–1753). Vatican II opens its teaching on the Church with Christ as the light of the nations, a light that shines out on the face of the Church (Lumen Gentium 1).

qa: Can a baptised believer really lose faith, as Hebrews warns?

Yes. Faith is God's gift, but we can lose it if we do not care for it. The Catechism says that to live, grow and persevere in faith we must nourish it with the word of God and beg the Lord to increase it (CCC 162). Hebrews does not aim to frighten but to keep us near each other and near God.
study: Who is the person I should encourage “today”, so that he or she is not worn down?
What do I look at most in a day: on my phone, in people, in myself? Is this filling me with light?
